newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: CASH COCOA LANGUISHES IN EUROPE BUT STG DIP HELPS.
newsitem.headline: CASH COCOA LANGUISHES IN EUROPE BUT STG DIP HELPS.

text.p: Europe's cash cocoa trade has been languishing in summer doldrums this week, but sterling's dip from recent peaks has prompted some industry offtake, traders said on Thursday.

The Continental Europe trade, particularly in Germany, took the opportunity to fill gaps in cover but quantities were minor, as many have plants shut for routine summer maintenance or are ticking over on holiday-thinned staffing levels.
"We're into a routine trading period, you only have to look at the turnover on London to see that, but the better currency situation has sparked a little buying," one trader commented.
A fall in September futures to 994 stg a tonne in London on Tuesday has also helped the cash trade, although trade buying on the lows has since taken the position back above 1,000 stg.
The Ivory Coast has been a routine seller into European cash markets, and is believed to be well sold on its upcoming 1997/98 main crop as well as some of the 1998/99 crop.
Traders said the country had sold at least 700,000 tonnes of the upcoming main crop and around 100,000 tonnes of the 1998/99 harvest.
"They are well sold right into 1999," one trader said.

Differentials for Ivorian cocoa have varied with sterling's swings, with traders pegging them anywhere between 50 stg and 20 stg under the terminal market. Ghana cocoa differentials have slipped under slack demand, fetching around 15 stg under.
The market is still monitoring the weather situation in the Ivory Coast, but the consensus view was that there were few problems there after recent rainfall.
"So far, so good. There's enough rain and the crop is shaping up nicely," said one trader.

The trade is also waiting to see what results from talks next week between a visiting International Monetary Fund mission to Abidjan. The country has already loosened its control over cocoa marketing but donors are expected to take a tougher stance and demand that the private sector plays a grater role in the export auction system.

In Europe, cocoa arrivals have slowed to snail's pace, and stock levels have continued to dwindle. According to the latest data from warehousing firm SGS, Amsterdam's inventories at the end of July were 513,000 tonnes, down 17,000 on a month earlier.
